title: Vatican II (1962–65)
hook: the Catholic Church opens its windows: Mass in local languages, new respect for other churches

segments.voice: Yesterday, Winona, singing on a stopped bus. Your line was this little light. What did you take out from under the basket? Day nine hundred sixty-three.

A small book with a ribbon in it, worn soft at the corners. It's an old Catholic missal, and on each page the prayers of the Mass run in two columns: Latin on one side, the local language on the other. For a long time, Catholics of the Western church heard the Mass in Latin, whether they lived in Manila or Milwaukee, and followed along in books like this one. Then a pope, John the Twenty-Third, called the bishops of the world to Rome for a council. A story often told has him opening a window to show what he hoped it would do: let in fresh air. Today, the council that came of it.

The Second Vatican Council met in Rome over several autumns, and the bishops wrote a set of documents that changed ordinary church life. Take four of them in turn. First, worship. The council allowed the Mass to be said in local languages, and asked that the people take a full, active part in it, not only watch. Soon parishes around the world were hearing the prayers in their own tongue. Some Catholics heard in this an echo of Pentecost in the book of Acts, where, in the King James Bible, "every man heard them speak in his own language." Second, scripture. The council urged that the Bible be opened wide to ordinary Catholics, read, prayed and studied, not left to the clergy. Third, other Christians. The council spoke of Protestant and Orthodox Christians with new warmth, as brothers and sisters in Christ, still separated, and called Catholics to pray and work for unity. Fourth, other faiths. In a short document, the council said that the Catholic Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in other religions. And it said plainly that the death of Christ cannot be charged against all the Jews of his time, or against Jews today, and it deplored hatred of Jews. Catholics still discuss how to read the council. Some see a long-overdue renewal. Some feel that beauty and reverence were lost along the way, and some parishes still celebrate the older Latin Mass with permission. Both groups are reading the same documents. That is part of what a council leaves behind.
screen: `RESPECT FOR OTHER FAITHS, AND FOR JEWS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one thing Vatican II changed. Settle, and breathe. Choose one of the four: the language of worship, the Bible in ordinary hands, other Christians, other faiths. Sit with it. If you're Catholic, think about the next Mass you'll attend, and the words you'll hear in your own language. If you're not, think about what it would be like to hear the prayers at the center of someone's week in a language they understood, or didn't. If you pray, you can pray in whatever words are truly yours. The bell holds the time.
Vatican II. The Catholic Church's Second Vatican Council, which brought the Mass into local languages and spoke with new respect of other churches and faiths.
Your line: open the windows. Today, open one: to a person, an idea, or a church you've kept at arm's length. Just let some air in. Day nine hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Catholic parishes today celebrate Mass in local languages, with readings from both Testaments, while some parishes also celebrate the older Latin form.

what a scholar hears: great constitutions on worship and scripture, and a short declaration that reshaped Catholic teaching about Jews, still read in more than one way inside the church.

notes: Council documents are under copyright in modern translation: all paraphrased. Confirm: vernacular permitted and 'full and active participation' (Sacrosanctum Concilium); scripture opened to the faithful (Dei Verbum); 'separated brethren' (Unitatis Redintegratio); 'rejects nothing that is true and holy' and the passage on Jews (Nostra Aetate 2 and 4).
Claims rule: no dates or counts of bishops or sessions ('over several autumns' instead). The title's years are the index's.
The window-opening story is hedged as 'a story often told'; it is probably apocryphal; confirm wording.
'Catholics of the Western church heard the Mass in Latin' refers to the Roman rite; Eastern Catholic churches used other languages. Confirm phrasing.
'Some Catholics heard in this an echo of Pentecost' is an interpretive line; confirm or cut.
Older Latin Mass 'with permission': current rules on the Traditional Latin Mass are contested and have changed; confirm phrasing.
Original: διάλεκτος (Acts 2:6, his own language); confirm spelling and pronunciation.
Editor pass: practice superlative ('the most important words of your week') reworded so it doesn't assume what matters most to the listener.
